final_proof:
The phrase “half are men and half are women” has two possible mathematical meanings, and they must be distinguished. If the sexes of all individuals are independent fair random variables, then the number of men is not identically half the population (although its expectation is half). Conversely, conditioning on exactly half being men destroys independence. Under the independent model the two expectations in the question are equal; under the exactly-balanced model women have a precisely quantifiable advantage.

Let the finite population be a set \(V\) of \(N\) labelled individuals, partitioned into fixed nonempty families. For \(i\in V\), let \(F(i)\) be the family of \(i\), let \(n_i=|F(i)|\), and put
\[
A=\frac1N\sum_{i\in V}(n_i-1)=\frac1N\sum_F |F|(|F|-1).
\]
Thus \(A\) is the expected number of siblings of an individual chosen uniformly from the population. Choose \(I\) uniformly from \(V\), independently of all sex assignments, and let \(B_I\) denote the number of brothers of \(I\).

First use the natural independent model: for every \(i\), let \(X_i\) be the indicator that \(i\) is male, and suppose that the \(X_i\) are independent with \(\Pr(X_i=1)=1/2\). For either \(x\in\{0,1\}\), and for every fixed \(i\), independence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E(B_I\mid I=i,X_i=x)
&=\mathbb E\left(\sum_{j\in F(i)\setminus\{i\}}X_j\,\middle|\,X_i=x\right)\\
&=\sum_{j\in F(i)\setminus\{i\}}\frac12
=\frac{n_i-1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, conditioning on \(X_I=x\) does not bias the choice of the label \(I\), since
\[
\Pr(I=i\mid X_I=x)=\frac{\Pr(I=i)\Pr(X_i=x)}{\Pr(X_I=x)}=\frac{(1/N)(1/2)}{1/2}=\frac1N.
\]
Averaging the preceding conditional expectation over \(i\) therefore yields
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is female})=\mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is male})=\frac A2.}
\]
No knowledge of the family-size distribution is needed. The same proof, with \(1/2\) replaced by \(p\), shows equality whenever the sexes are independent and identically distributed with male probability \(p\).

Here is also the answer under the alternative model in which there are exactly as many men as women. Suppose \(N=2M\), and choose the set of the \(M\) male labels uniformly from all \(M\)-subsets of \(V\). This assignment is exchangeable but not independent. Given that \(I=i\) is female, all \(M\) male labels lie among the other \(N-1\) people, so each particular sibling of \(i\) has conditional probability \(M/(N-1)\) of being male. Given that \(I=i\) is male, only \(M-1\) male labels remain, so that probability is \((M-1)/(N-1)\). By symmetry, conditional on either sex the label \(I\) is still uniform on \(V\). Consequently
\[
\mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is female})=A\frac{M}{N-1},\qquad \mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is male})=A\frac{M-1}{N-1},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is female})-\mathbb E(B_I\mid I\text{ is male})=\frac{A}{N-1}.}
\]
Thus the intuition that a male “uses up” one of the available males is valid only in this fixed-total model, precisely because the sex variables are then dependent.

Finally, the proposed within-family averaging argument is invalid because the two population averages use different weights for the families. In a family with \(b\) boys and \(g\) girls, each girl has \(b\) brothers and each boy has \(b-1\) brothers. But that family's contribution is weighted by \(g\) when one samples a girl and by \(b\) when one samples a boy. Those weights need not be the same.

For a concrete refutation, take two families of size \(101\). Let the first contain \(100\) boys and one girl and the second contain one boy and \(100\) girls. There are equally many boys and girls overall. Within each family every girl has exactly one more brother than every boy in that family. Nevertheless, the girls' mean number of brothers is
\[
\frac{1\cdot100+100\cdot1}{101}=\frac{200}{101},
\]
whereas the boys' mean is
\[
\frac{100\cdot99+1\cdot0}{101}=\frac{9900}{101}.
\]
So even the direction can reverse after averaging. This does not conflict with the equality of conditional expectations in the independent random-sex model: the displayed configuration is one possible realized assignment, while the equality proved above averages over all independent assignments (as well as the uniformly selected individual).
